clinicalPearls: Two major subsets: limited cutaneous SSc (lcSSc) with skin confined to fingers, distal limbs and face (trunk spared) and an indolent course; and diffuse cutaneous SSc (dcSSc) with rapidly progressive skin involvement of fingers, extremities, face and trunk (p.2859, 2866).

In lcSSc, Raynaud's phenomenon typically precedes sclerodactyly and other manifestations, sometimes by years; the CREST constellation (calcinosis cutis, Raynaud's, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia) is a distinct lcSSc subset (p.2859).
Bilateral symmetrical skin thickening starting in the fingers and advancing distal-to-proximal is the hallmark distinguishing SSc from other connective tissue diseases (p.2867).

SSc-specific autoantibodies are mutually exclusive and aid risk stratification: anti-centromere is associated with lcSSc and isolated PAH (renal crisis rare); anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) with dcSSc, extensive skin, early ILD and cardiac involvement; anti-RNA polymerase III with rapidly progressive skin, renal crisis and contemporaneous cancer (p.2864, 2871).
Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are detectable in virtually all SSc patients, even in early/preclinical stages (p.2864, 2871).

Nailfold capillaroscopy distinguishes primary Raynaud's disease (regular, evenly spaced parallel hairpin loops) from secondary Raynaud's/SSc (giant capillaries, dilated and distorted loops, microhemorrhages, capillary dropout) and helps establish early SSc diagnosis (p.2867, 2871).
ILD and pulmonary vascular disease together account for the majority of SSc-related deaths; survival is particularly poor when both coexist (p.2868).

Scleroderma renal crisis presents with accelerated hypertension plus acute kidney injury, occurs in <15% of patients almost always within 4 years of onset, and is associated with diffuse/progressive skin involvement and anti-RNA polymerase III (up to 50%); anti-centromere appears protective (p.2870-2871).
Palpable tendon friction rubs are associated with increased risk of renal and cardiac complications and reduced survival, and may be a harbinger of impending renal crisis (p.2871).
SSc patients should be screened for PAH at initial evaluation and annually thereafter, and screened for ILD with regular pulmonary monitoring for several years after diagnosis (p.2868, 2872).
SSc sine scleroderma: characteristic Raynaud's plus typical clinical/serologic features of SSc in the absence of detectable skin thickening (~10% of patients) (p.2859, 2866, 2872).
harrison.pathophysiology: SSc is a chronic, often progressive disease of unknown etiology defined pathologically by widespread microangiopathy (fibroproliferative vasculopathy with capillary loss and obliteration) combined with multiorgan fibrosis, on a background of autoimmunity. An initial vascular insult in a genetically predisposed individual (modest HLA class II and immune-regulatory gene associations) triggers inflammation, generation of SSc-specific autoantibodies, and sustained activation of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts driven by mediators such as TGF-beta, IL-6, CTGF, PDGF and endothelin. Maladaptive repair leads to replacement of normal tissue with rigid, avascular, acellular connective tissue affecting skin, lungs, heart, GI tract, kidneys and other organs (p.2859-2866).
additionalDifferentials: Localized scleroderma (morphea, linear scleroderma, coup de sabre) - generally not complicated by Raynaud's or internal organ involvement (p.2860, 2871)
Mixed connective tissue disease and SSc overlap syndromes (with polymyositis, Sjogren's, SLE, polyarthritis, autoimmune liver disease) (p.2860, 2866)
Primary Raynaud's disease - benign, must be differentiated from early/limited SSc (p.2867, 2871)
nonInfectiousMimics: Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (associated with gadolinium exposure) (p.2860)
Vinyl chloride-induced disease and other chemically/drug-associated scleroderma-like conditions (p.2860)
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura / thrombotic microangiopathy - scleroderma renal crisis is sometimes initially misdiagnosed as TTP (p.2871)
additionalInvestigations: ANA and SSc-specific autoantibodies (anti-centromere, anti-topoisomerase I/Scl-70, anti-RNA polymerase III, U3-RNP/fibrillarin, Th/To, PM/Scl) for diagnosis and risk stratification (p.2864, 2871)
Nailfold capillaroscopy (low-power stereomicroscope or videocapillaroscopy under immersion oil) (p.2867)
High-resolution chest CT (HRCT) for ILD detection and prognostic assessment of fibrosis extent (p.2868)
Pulmonary function testing including FVC and DLCO for ILD monitoring (a DLCO reduction out of proportion to lung volumes suggests pulmonary vascular disease) (p.2868)
Doppler echocardiography for PAH screening; right heart (cardiac) catheterization to confirm PAH and exclude venoocclusive/postcapillary causes (p.2868)
NT-proBNP correlates with presence/severity of PAH and survival (not specific) (p.2868-2869, 2871)
Cardiac MRI / tissue Doppler / SPECT for occult myocardial involvement (p.2871)
Blood film for microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, platelet count, urinalysis and creatinine in suspected renal crisis (p.2871)
redFlags: Scleroderma renal crisis: accelerated/new hypertension (generally >150/90 mmHg) with progressive oliguric renal failure - a medical emergency (note ~10% present normotensive, with poorer outcome) (p.2870-2871)
Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with fragmented red cells and thrombocytopenia (hallmark of renal crisis) (p.2871)
New unexplained anemia, thrombocytopenia, pericardial effusion or new tendon friction rubs as harbingers of impending renal crisis (p.2871)
Pulmonary arterial hypertension: exertional dyspnea, near-syncope, loud P2, right heart failure - 3-year survival of untreated PAH <50% (p.2868)
Rapidly progressive ILD with declining FVC (can fall ~30%/year), most rapid in the first 3-5 years (p.2868)
Critical digital ischemia with fingertip ulceration/necrosis and acro-osteolysis (p.2867)
harrison.prognosis: Highly variable; dcSSc carries a more rapidly progressive course and worse prognosis than lcSSc. SSc confers a fivefold to eightfold higher age/sex-adjusted mortality, with median survival ~11 years; 5- and 10-year survival are ~70%/55% in dcSSc and ~90%/75% in lcSSc. Major causes of death are PAH, pulmonary fibrosis, GI involvement and cardiac disease. Scleroderma renal crisis carries ~30% 3-year mortality (markedly improved by ACE inhibitors). Poor-prognosis markers include male sex, African ancestry, older age at onset, extensive truncal skin involvement, palpable tendon friction rubs, significant/progressive visceral involvement, and laboratory findings of elevated ESR, anemia, proteinuria and anti-topoisomerase I antibodies (p.2873).
pitfalls: Early dcSSc may present with only upper-extremity edema and puffy fingers and Raynaud's may be absent, leading to misdiagnosis as arthritis, SLE, myositis or undifferentiated connective tissue disease (p.2872)
Scleroderma renal crisis can be misdiagnosed as TTP or other thrombotic microangiopathy; renal biopsy and von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease activity may help (p.2871)
Glucocorticoids (especially prednisone >=10 mg/d) are associated with precipitating scleroderma renal crisis and should be used only when essential and at low dose in high-risk patients (p.2870)
PFTs and conventional echocardiography are relatively insensitive for early ILD and early cardiac involvement, respectively (p.2868, 2871)
Echocardiography can over- or underestimate pulmonary artery pressures, so PAH must be confirmed by cardiac catheterization (p.2868)
SSc sine scleroderma can be missed because diagnostic skin induration is absent despite organ involvement (p.2872)
harrison.severityClassification: ACR/EULAR classification criteria are >90% specific and sensitive but are intended for research rather than clinical practice; weighted items include skin thickening proximal to MCP joints (score 9), sclerodactyly/puffy fingers, fingertip lesions, telangiectasia, abnormal nailfold capillaries, ILD/PAH, Raynaud's phenomenon, and SSc-specific autoantibodies (anti-centromere, Scl-70, RNA polymerase III). Clinically, patients are stratified into limited cutaneous and diffuse cutaneous subsets by extent of skin involvement (p.2860).
management: Vasodilator therapy for Raynaud phenomenon and digital ulcers, using calcium channel blockers, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, and endothelin receptor antagonists or prostacyclin analogues for severe ischaemia
Immunosuppression for skin and interstitial lung disease with mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, or rituximab and tocilizumab, adding the antifibrotic nintedanib for progressive fibrosis
Targeted pulmonary vasodilator therapy for pulmonary arterial hypertension, guided by right heart catheterisation
Prompt ACE-inhibitor therapy for scleroderma renal crisis, while avoiding high-dose glucocorticoids that precipitate it
Proton pump inhibitors and prokinetics for reflux and gastrointestinal dysmotility
Structured surveillance with pulmonary function tests and echocardiography to detect lung and pulmonary vascular disease early
Multidisciplinary care across rheumatology, respiratory, cardiology and gastroenterology
